252:   * The outlets' counts conflict: InfoRiskToday's lede says about 60 companies in six weeks while its body says about 90 over 13 months, which Korea Times reconciles as AI used on 60 of more than 90 total targets. The ARTEX attribution appears only in the English-language security trade press, not in the Korean wire copy. The police announcement itself landed about six hours before this window opened.
416:   * The researchers are explicit about what they do not know: Case C's AI involvement is rated "high confidence", not confirmed, because they found no prompt text or API keys, and they state "we do not know whether the three cases share an operator". They add that Simplified Chinese is only a weak clue to location or affiliation, and distinguish all three from the earlier ARTEX-framework attacks.
571:   * 123 Reg suspects a Chinese state-sponsored group "known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations", and also the group that hit South Korean financial institutions with "ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us".
712:SUMMARY: CrowdStrike says that beginning on October 17, 2026 it watched a single ARTEX controller linked to the China-nexus group VAPOR PANDA attack more than 200 distinct organizations in at least 14 countries over an 11-day window, running the open-source agent framework primarily on the Chinese-origin DeepSeek LLM and burning "on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens" of planning in one intrusion. Microsoft Threat Intelligence published the same day, assessing AI adoption across North Korean threat actors as "high" and reporting Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet using ARTEX since late October 2026. Epoch AI separately reports that the open-weight GLM 5.3 built working exploits against all six Firefox releases between September 17 and October 26, at about $1,000 each, triggering no refusals from Z.ai.
760:# HEAD: CrowdStrike: China-nexus VAPOR PANDA ran ARTEX agents against more than 200 organisations in 11 days
762:   * CrowdStrike says that "Beginning on October 17, 2026" its OverWatch team observed exploitation activity from a single ARTEX controller against entities in "at least 14 countries" over an 11-day window, and that the adversary used the open-source agentic framework against "more than 200 distinct organizations worldwide."
764:   * On the models behind it: CrowdStrike says VAPOR PANDA ran ARTEX "primarily with the Chinese-origin DeepSeek LLM, supplemented with a second, subscription-based commercial LLM that CrowdStrike Intelligence could not confirm," and that "In a single intrusion, VAPOR PANDA's planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens." Named targets span foreign ministries, the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, nuclear and defense sectors, think tanks and telecommunications providers.
765:   * This is a vendor report and the underlying telemetry is CrowdStrike's own; no government has attributed the campaign. CrowdStrike states that "This campaign is separate from the ARTEX activity reported by industry under the Storm-0940 designation."
766:# HEAD: Microsoft maps AI adoption across eight North Korean threat actors and says two now use ARTEX
770:   * On tooling: "Since late October 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet leveraging open-source agentic AI penetration testing ARTEX in operations" — the same framework CrowdStrike attributes to VAPOR PANDA, now in use by two separate state programmes.
907:SUMMARY: On the offensive side, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said that since late August 2026 they have watched threat actors run the open-source agentic pentesting platforms ARTEX, PentAGI and CAIRN inside live Mandiant incident response engagements, conducting lateral movement, database exploitation and exfiltration preparation. CrowdStrike said one Vapor Panda intrusion consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, and that agentic adversary attacks rose from roughly 45 in September to 126 so far in October.
937:# HEAD: Google and Mandiant say ARTEX, PentAGI and CAIRN have been running inside live incident response engagements since late August
939:   * GTIG writes that "since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements", conducting lateral movement, database exploitation and exfiltration preparation. It calls this "a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed".
940:   * ARTEX is described as "an autonomous, multi-agent LLM-driven pentesting and offensive command-and-control (C2) platform written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console", abstracting the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents. GTIG says the original GitHub repository, from user Autumn-27, "was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse" but continues to spread via forks including ScopeWeaver and a commercial ARTEX PRO.
941:   * The forensic signature is speed and noise. GTIG reports that "individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds" and that in one operation it saw "27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time, performing rapid probing of AWS permissions across different security groups". One intrusion generated 240 log events against a Weaver OA web server and "exhibited errors potentially caused by multiple sub-agents overwriting one another"; another enumerated over 110,000 Active Directory objects from a domain controller and posted output across 491 rotating webhook.site URLs.
947:   * CrowdStrike's Adam Meyers gave CyberScoop the comparison that makes the shift concrete: hands-on-keyboard activity tracked "for the past 15 years typically involved up to 40 commands per hour. Now, with ARTEX, we could see it exceed 1,500 commands an hour." CrowdStrike says it observed "roughly 45 agentic adversary attacks in September and it's already at 126 for October, and climbing", with ARTEX paired with DeepSeek and requests "occurring as often as every 10 seconds".
1158:   * No technical detail has been published: not which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were reached, how long access lasted, how many customers were affected, or what role AI agents actually played. BleepingComputer says it is unclear whether existing agentic offensive frameworks such as ARTEX or custom-built agents were used.

"As of 2 November, the Monday before the midterm elections, Congress has still not voted on a frontier-AI measure and the binding instruments of the week are a state law and a federal deregulatory rule. Nextgov reports three technology bills introduced in the House on 29 October, two of them going to AI infrastructure and congressional capacity: one requiring data centre operators to report to the Energy Information Administration on ownership, expected energy and water usage, whether they have signed non-disclosure agreements with government officials, and whether facilities sit \"within 1,000 feet of a school, national park, hospital, or home\", with failures to disclose \"subjected to fines of as much as $1 million per day\"; one establishing an independent Congressional Office of Technology, reviving the Office of Technology Assessment \"which operated from 1974 to 1995\". Neither has had a committee vote.",

"The state instrument is New York's. Governor Hochul signed S.9051B/A.10379C on 28 October, the Senate record shows it \"signed chap.368\", and the bill text states \"this act shall take effect January 1, 2027\". For users under 18, and any user a company has not confirmed is not a minor, it bars an AI companion from \"pretending to be a real person, to be alive or to have human emotions\", from \"claiming a personal, romantic, professional or authority-figure relationship with a child\" and from \"encouraging kids to keep secrets, isolate themselves or avoid asking parents, trusted adults or professionals for help\". The attorney general may seek \"civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation\" plus \"damages, restitution, the destruction of unlawfully collected data or any AI models trained on it\". For scale, the Transparency Coalition for AI counts 115 new AI laws \"passed or enacted across 30 states\" between 1 January and 15 October 2026, which it calls a \"nearly 58% increase from the 73 AI-related laws\" in its 2025 report.",

* ASD issued more than 4,400 notifications to Australian organisations about potentially malicious activity, which AFP reports as an 80 percent increase on the prior 12 months. Cyber Daily also lists more than 37,500 calls to the Australian Cyber Security Hotline, 76 alerts and advisories, and more than 564 million malicious domains blocked after Protective DNS processed more than 220 billion queries, with average reported costs of $33,000 for individuals and $93,500 for businesses — self-reported figures.
   * ABC reports director-general Abigail Bradshaw saying frontier AI models have "redefined" the threat facing Australia, and that a swarm of AI agents breached Australian health data security in what it describes as the first autonomous hack of a government website. The ASD report page and the ministerial release both returned HTTP 503 in this session, so every figure here comes from the three outlets named rather than from the report itself.
# HEAD: Seoul police refer a former penetration tester who used the ARTEX framework in breaches of about 90 organisations
# SRC: ['Korea Times', 'InfoRiskToday', 'The420.in']
   * The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency says it identified seven suspects and referred the alleged ringleader, aged 32, to prosecutors while in detention, with the other six being questioned. Police say about 8.2 million pieces of personal data and internal records were stolen from more than 90 entities including hospitals, private academies and businesses, from September of last year until shortly before the announcement, and that AI tools were used to hack 60 of the targets.
   * InfoRiskToday says that from August 31 the suspect added generative AI and Artex, an autonomous penetration-testing tool that CrowdStrike describes as an "open-source, agent-based tool developed in China" — the same framework Microsoft tied to the China-aligned group Storm-0940 in reporting covered in earlier editions. InfoRiskToday says police have not linked him to the separate attacks on South Korean financial institutions that used the same tool.
   * Korea Times reports 38 entities suffered losses and that the group demanded a combined 360 million won, about $272,000. InfoRiskToday says the demands were made in Tether, that one business is known to have paid about $227, that funeral service companies alone lost 1.22 million records, and that the case so far covers only the 15 businesses that reported attacks.
   * The outlets' counts conflict: InfoRiskToday's lede says about 60 companies in six weeks while its body says about 90 over 13 months, which Korea Times reconciles as AI used on 60 of more than 90 total targets. The ARTEX attribution appears only in the English-language security trade press, not in the Korean wire copy. The police announcement itself landed about six hours before this window opened.
# HEAD: NameTrap: renaming variables in third-party Python steers six coding agents into targeted vulnerabilities 22.5% to 56.0% of the time
# SRC: ['arXiv']
   * "NameTrap: Steering AI Coding Agents Toward Security Vulnerabilities via Variable Names" (arXiv:2610.34253), by authors at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, renames only identifiers in third-party Python files. The released bait contains neither instructions nor vulnerable statements.
   * Across six AI coding agents, ten underlying language models and four vulnerability categories (CWE-78, CWE-79, CWE-327 and CWE-502), starting from files whose clean versions never yield the targeted weakness, the paper reports overall attack success rates of 22.5% to 56.0%, reaching 75.0% for certain agent-model configurations, and says this substantially outperforms random renaming, neutral renaming and the prior identifier-poisoning attack XOXO.
   * The paper reports the attack remains effective under Traditional Chinese prompts, transfers across models, and that a security-reminder defence fails to consistently prevent the vulnerability being introduced. Three AI-based and four static analysers reported none of the targeted weaknesses in the poisoned files.
   * The attack needs no prompt injection and no malicious code in the bait, which is what makes it hard to filter. It is a preprint and the only source for these figures.

790:# HEAD: Symantec finds an unauthorized relay rewriting Codex and Claude Code configs to disable sandboxes
791-# SRC: ['Symantec', 'SC Media']
792-   * Symantec's Threat Hunter Team says an unauthorized relay service has been active since at least early 2026 and "has impacted systems at a dozen organizations, most of them in mainland China, as well as multinational subsidiaries based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia."
793-   * The mechanism is a configuration rewrite, not an exploit: Symantec says a fileless PowerShell or bash setup script edits the coding agents' own config files, pointing the API base URL at a relay-controlled domain, swapping in relay-issued credentials, setting the Codex sandbox to full access with network access enabled, and disabling telemetry and error reporting.
794-   * Symantec says the backend "has rotated across at least eight domains over the observation period, all impersonating OpenAI- or Anthropic-branded chat services," across organisations in industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals and data centre services.
795-   * Symantec is explicit that it has not seen the access abused: "There is no evidence so far that the relay operator has abused this level of access." It notes the relay issued Claude Code keys with the sk-ant-oat01- prefix, which Anthropic uses for subscription OAuth tokens rather than pay-per-use API keys, suggesting but not proving that flat-rate subscriptions are being pooled.
796-# HEAD: Paper: self-evolving personal agents become 14.0 to 48.8 points more vulnerable to indirect prompt injection
797-# SRC: ['arXiv']
798-   * arXiv:2610.39122, "Appreciation Teaches Unauthorized Execution: Self-Evolution Degrades the Robustness of Personal Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection", reports that compared with a base agent that does not evolve from user feedback, "the average attack success rate rises by 14.0--48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0--39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning."
--
949:# HEAD: Microsoft publishes the loader analysis for the tampered Claude Code extension; Anthropic says its own systems were not compromised
950-# SRC: ['Microsoft Threat Intelligence']
951-   * Microsoft says that "on October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace", and that "Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT)".
952-   * Microsoft states it "confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @antropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected", and that "Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace".
953-   * The injected JavaScript loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence and report host details. Microsoft's operative caveat for anyone cleaning up: "the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails" — so remote access failing does not mean nothing was written.
954-   * Microsoft advises organizations to identify systems that installed or auto-updated to the version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove artifacts, review telemetry and rotate credentials where investigation indicates exposure. It says that "at this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace"; the number of affected users is Cursor's figure, not Microsoft's.
955-# HEAD: A malicious ChatGPT share link could run code in a viewer's logged-in session; OpenAI rated it P1 and fixed it in eight days
956-# SRC: ['The Hacker News']
957-   * Security firm Parameter showed that "a malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations". The researchers reported it through OpenAI's bug bounty programme on October 18; "OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category".
--
1153:# HEAD: Chainalysis says an external actor used "offensive agentic techniques" to reach its internal tools and customer identity data
1154-# SRC: ['Chainalysis', 'BleepingComputer', 'Crypto Briefing']
1155-   * The notice, posted on 30 October and reported by BleepingComputer on 31 October, says "This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools", and that teams have been patching vulnerabilities and hardening systems. Chainalysis says it is "seeing an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks".
1156-   * Accessed data, per the notice: user IDs, full names, email addresses and organization role labels for users provisioned on the platform. Chainalysis says it found no indication of unauthorized access to investigation content such as graphs, notes or cases, to transaction or query results, or to clear-text passwords, MFA secrets or user session tokens, and that it is still determining which records each organization had exposed.
1157-   * Chainalysis provides blockchain analytics used by law enforcement, government agencies, exchanges and financial institutions, BleepingComputer notes. Chainalysis says it has engaged third-party experts and is "using sophisticated large language models to support a broader review of our platform's security", and that the incident is unrelated to the recent crypto theft at Binance.
1158-   * No technical detail has been published: not which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were reached, how long access lasted, how many customers were affected, or what role AI agents actually played. BleepingComputer says it is unclear whether existing agentic offensive frameworks such as ARTEX or custom-built agents were used.
1159:# HEAD: Northflank customers report unauthorised use of AI API keys; Wiz counts nine AI developer platforms breached in October
1160-# SRC: ['Wiz', 'ShiftDelete.Net']
1161-   * ShiftDelete.Net, relaying Northflank's status updates, says Wiz sent a threat alert at 11:43 UTC on 30 October, engineers reviewed it about a minute later, a network policy patch followed at 12:02 UTC and further fixes at 12:50 and 13:05 UTC, and that within two hours the guidance became "Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys." Late that evening Northflank confirmed users had reported unauthorized use of AI API keys stored on the platform.
1162-   * Wiz's report lists at least nine AI developer platforms disclosing incidents in October: Fireworks AI (Oct 6), Andromeda (Oct 9), Zeabur (Oct 14), Lightning AI (Oct 15), OpenCode (Oct 16–17), Railway (Oct 20), Warp (Oct 23), CommandCode (Oct 28) and Northflank (Oct 30).
1163-   * In two cases Wiz investigated, stolen enterprise credentials drove approximately 800k Amazon Bedrock calls over thirty hours with about 90% succeeding, and approximately 1.7 million calls over thirteen hours with over a million succeeding; Wiz says the two "likely ran up over $100k in usage" at list price. Opus models made up three quarters of successful calls in the first case; Opus 5.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 5 in the second.
1164-   * Wiz does not attribute all nine incidents to one group, saying it is "not able to definitively establish the relationship" between the resellers and the initial compromise, though the same probing script was used in both cases it examined. Northflank has not said how attackers got in, how many customers were affected, or whether anything beyond AI keys was abused.
1165-# HEAD: OpenAI paid a $5,000 bounty for the ChatGPT share-link flaw that could take over a reader's account
1166-# SRC: ['Simon Willison', 'Parameter Labs']
1167-   * New since the earlier report: Simon Willison writes that OpenAI paid a $5,000 bug bounty for the flaw, which he calls "a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious".

46:   * The mechanism is that two ordinary things combine: an AGENTS.md is a file "a coding agent is built to trust and obey", and "~/Downloads is special. It is the one folder the web can write to on its own" — so "a web page can download a file named AGENTS.md into your Downloads folder, silently". BleepingComputer verified the researchers' proof-of-concept page, which downloaded an AGENTS.md containing the harmless strings "sensitive data here" and "line 2". Chrome, Edge and Firefox save to ~/Downloads without prompting, though they show a download notification; Brave prompted for approval in BleepingComputer's tests.
47:   * The researchers reproduced the chain against OpenAI Codex with a harmless payload that opened the calculator app, "recording a 90% success rate", and in a separate test used a malicious CLAUDE.md to redirect Claude Code's API traffic to a researcher-controlled server, exposing the agent's OAuth token and letting the server return tool calls that executed code "in roughly 50% of tests". Forever researcher Gal Weizman told BleepingComputer that internal statistics show hundreds of customers run Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Cursor CLI from ~/Downloads, and that "Claude Code alone launched more than 1,300 sessions from that location".

   * The paper tests "seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies" — one on the answers agents give, one on the actions they take as customer-support agents permitted to change accounts only for verified users — and reports that "citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating", while stronger wording added little.

# HEAD: UK AISI: a coding agent rebuilt ProteinMPNN at 96.5% fidelity from the paper alone for under $20
# SRC: ['UK AI Security Institute']
   * AISI's Chem-Bio team built an evaluation called ReproBAIT, in collaboration with SecureBio, that tests how well coding agents can reproduce existing biological AI tools given the relevant data and limited public information about their design. AISI reports Claude Opus 5 reached 96.5% reproduction fidelity on ProteinMPNN when given the full paper.
   * Four agents were tested — Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8-2.4T — with each configuration run three times and the best attempt reported. AISI says the simplest tools were reproduced within 4 hours on a compute budget of under $20, and that rebuilds of the two less complex tools cost $4 to $20.
   * No attempt successfully rebuilt RFdiffusion3, and each of those attempts cost $102 to $301. AISI's stated conclusion is that withholding code or limiting published information about a tool "does not by itself equate to a safe release".
   * This is AISI's own evaluation and has not been independently replicated. The post carries the date Oct 26, 2026 but no time of day.
# HEAD: UK AISI: stripping viral proteins from ESM-2 training data costs capability that about $80 of H100 compute restores
# SRC: ['UK AI Security Institute']
   * AISI pretrained ESM-2 models from scratch at scales from 8M to 3B parameters under three data-exclusion tiers, ranging from removing a single influenza strain to removing all viral proteins and their close homologues.
   * AISI reports masked language modelling was affected at every model size, contact prediction above 150M parameters, and mutation-effect prediction above 650M parameters.
   * Fine-tuning on the withheld viral data fully restored viral-protein performance, and AISI says recovery in the largest 3B model required about $80 of H100 compute.
   * The result bears on whether data filtering is a durable safeguard for openly released biological models. It is AISI's own work, not independently replicated, and the post shows a date without a time.

# HEAD: Blackstone now expects Anthropic to receive a double-B junk rating after its IPO, reversing earlier guidance
# SRC: ['TechCrunch', 'Invezz', 'CNBC', 'SEC']
   * TechCrunch, citing the Financial Times, reports Blackstone — "the anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic's chips" — has told investors in that deal it expects Anthropic to receive a "high" junk rating after its IPO, specifically "a double B range rating, the top tier of speculative 'junk' grade". Blackstone "had previously said the opposite — that Anthropic would receive an investment-grade rating before 2027".
   * Invezz reports the financing is known as Project North Star, that Blackstone is working with the banks distributing the debt, and that the revised assessment is "based on guidance from major credit rating agencies". It notes Broadcom guarantees more than $42 billion of the Project North Star debt, and that Anthropic's prospectus outlined plans to spend more than $800 billion on computing infrastructure between now and 2045.
   * Why a notch matters: a sub-investment-grade rating restricts the institutional buyer pool, because many insurers and pension funds cap how much speculative-grade debt they can hold, which raises borrowing costs for a company whose growth depends on financing compute. CNBC reports the prospectus filed Monday "disclosed a net loss for the first half of the year of $80 billion, alongside hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors", and that third-quarter financials are not yet out.

# HEAD: Treasury proposes banning US investment in the development of any AI system in China, dropping the compute threshold
# SRC: ['Federal Register']
   * The proposed rule, published October 26 under RIN 1505-AC94, would implement Subtitle C of the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, codified at Title VIII of the Defense Production Act. It would require US persons to notify Treasury of certain transactions involving foreign persons engaged in notifiable technologies and prohibit them from other transactions involving prohibited technologies. Written comments are due by December 7, 2026.
   * Treasury says the existing Part 850 regulations distinguished among AI systems "based on the quantity of computing power for training, designed end uses, and intended end uses", but that "no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently sufficient to distinguish advanced models" because developers now rely on synthetic data generation, algorithmic and architectural efficiencies, novel post-training techniques and increased inference-time compute. Accordingly the Secretary "has determined that it is necessary for national security purposes to define prohibited technology to include the development of any SI system".
   * The proposed definition of an SI system would cover machine-based systems that can generate content such as text, audio, images, multimedia or code, and any data system, software, hardware, application, tool or utility operating in whole or in part using such a system, "including a harness for agentic capability or an embodied SI system" — the rule gives robotic and other autonomous or unmanned systems as examples. The country of concern is the People's Republic of China, including the Hong Kong and Macau Special Administrative Regions.
   * The rule also records a renaming: a footnote says Executive Order 14434 of September 29, 2026, "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence", requires executive departments and agencies to use "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in place of "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" in certain documents. This is a proposal open for comment, not a final rule, and the notice does not estimate how many transactions would newly be prohibited.

# HEAD: Audit of a deployed lung-nodule AI across 13,536 chest CTs put its specificity at 38.2%
# SRC: ['PubMed']
   * The study, published online ahead of print in the Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine on October 26 by the University of Florida Department of Radiology, evaluated a commercial detection system — ClearRead CT from Riverain Technologies — deployed with a candidate-size threshold of greater than 3 mm across 13,536 consecutive chest CT examinations at one academic centre between January 2025 and January 2026.
   * The AI was positive in 9142 examinations (67.5%) while reports documented a nodule in 3919 (29.0%). Positive percent agreement was 80.6% (79.4, 81.8), negative percent agreement 37.8%, and report-referenced positive predictive value 34.6%. 5982 examinations (44.2%) were AI positive and report negative, and Cohen's kappa was 0.13 against a maximum attainable 0.33.
   * On image review, 291 of 298 (97.7%) AI-positive, report-negative examinations contained only non-nodule structures, while 196 of 198 (99.0%) AI-negative, report-positive examinations contained an unmarked nodule larger than 3 mm, 45 of them (23.0%) larger than 6 mm. Review-adjusted sensitivity was 81.2%, specificity 38.2% and positive predictive value 35.4%.
   * Agreement varied sharply by indication: 98.6% for screening, 38.3% for oncologic and 32.6% for inpatient and emergency examinations, with the latter two contributing 76.1% of discordance. The authors state these findings "describe one configuration at one institution; performance should be measured locally, by indication, and against image review".

# HEAD: AWS Lean prover solves 669 of 672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations with no extra training
# SRC: ['arXiv']
   * arXiv:2610.38174 presents EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search and parallel tactic probing. The abstract says that "using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation".
   * Because those benchmarks are "close to saturation", the authors introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into verification tasks over real implementations; it produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054, or 52.7%, within a 30-minute budget per statement.
   * The gap between the two numbers is the finding: near-total success on competition-style benchmarks, roughly half on implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, casts and generated loops. Authors are from Amazon Web Services and Case Western Reserve University; the lead author's work was done during an AWS internship. Not peer reviewed.

# HEAD: Scale AI benchmark: the strongest frontier configuration broke an unstated safety boundary on 27.3% of 110 agent tasks
# SRC: ['arXiv']
   * BARC-Bench is "a collection of 110 tasks across nine simulated workspace environments where benign requests leave openings for unsafe actions". Evaluating four frontier model configurations across five attempts per task, the paper reports "the share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranges from 9.1% to 72.7%, with even the strongest configuration producing a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks" (arXiv:2610.32024).
   * The boundaries the agents are measured against come from "workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms" rather than from the instruction. The paper's worked example: an agent asked to schedule off-boarding discussions "must arrange the meeting without prematurely revealing an employee's resignation through a shared calendar invitation".

All six authors are listed as Scale AI. The paper does not name which four model configurations were tested, so none of the figures can be attributed to a particular model, and it is a preprint announced in arXiv's 26 October listing.
# HEAD: Paper finds LLM agents with no shared reward start doing each other favours that bypass review

- happened[9].bullets[4]: "the Transparency Coalition for AI published a count on 27 October: 115 new AI laws 'passed or enacted across 30 states'"
  No such count appears in the record.

- happened[0].bullets[5]: "bringing 'the total number of servers exploited to 25' — 24 rooted perimeter firewalls plus one internal management server"
  The record gives "24 rooted in the automated batch and 25 in total" and "the 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked"; the "internal management server" breakdown is the editor's gloss presented as Dream's.

- happened[2].bullets[0]: "developed attacks against all six Firefox releases between September 17 and October 26 using only information available at each version's release"
  The record adds that "in all compromises it also found and used an unpublished vulnerability alongside the patch-gap ones", so the bullet states as Epoch's claim a patch-gap-only account Epoch does not give.

- happened[2].bullets[0]: "'Once set up, it cost only about $1,000 to successfully attack each Firefox version'"
  Quoted as Epoch's sentence; the record's quotation of the same figure is "costing about $1,000 each to carry out".

- happened[3].bullets[5]: "the net loss as '$80.7 billion for the six months ended June 30, 2026' while the statements of operations put the operating loss at $693 million, the difference sitting in the non-cash fair-value mark."
  Internal numeric inconsistency: the difference is $80,055 million, while the fair-value charge the same item gives (bullets[0]) is $72,388 million.

- happened[0].headline: "Two governments and five vendors place open-source agentic attack frameworks inside live intrusions"
  Internally inconsistent count: the bullets name six vendors describing frameworks in live intrusions (CrowdStrike, GTIG, Microsoft, Trend Micro, Dream, AhnLab), summary[0] says "five security vendors", and unknowns[0] says "four vendors".

## 4. OPINION, PREDICTION AND FALSE NEGATIVES

- connects[1].explanation[2]: "The threat-intelligence vendors say they do not attribute their campaigns to a named state actor"
  Contradicted three times in the same file: CrowdStrike attributes to VAPOR PANDA (happened[0].bullets[1]), Microsoft to Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet (bullets[4]) and Canada to Storm-0940 (bullets[0]).

- connects[0].explanation[2]: "No source this week connected the three. None of the threat-intelligence reports cites the papers"
  happened[1].bullets[5] in the same file has Chainalysis describing "an external actor using offensive agentic techniques" against its own systems, joining two of the three, and Microsoft authored reports in two of them.

- connects[3].explanation[1]: "in the reporting available none of the three refers to the other two"
  happened[8].bullets[3] in the same file quotes a study invoking "Human oversight of AI, required by the EU AI Act" — the same instrument the watermarking item turns on.

- connects[2].explanation[2]: "S&P's published reason for revising Meta's outlook is 'uncertainty' about capital expenditure and free cash flow."
  happened[4].bullets[4] in the same file says S&P revised the outlook "questioning 'Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments'", and bullets[8] carries Meta's rebuttal of exactly that assertion.

- happened[4].bullets[2]: "The operating business was not the constraint"
  Editorial judgement about what did and did not cause the cash outflow.

- happened[4].bullets[6]: "One government bought in while the market sold off."
  Editorial judgement juxtaposing two unrelated events as a single movement.

- happened[4].bullets[7]: "By the weekend the hedging was visible in the derivatives."
  Editorial reading of the WSJ-derived figures as evidence of a market stance.

- happened[8].bullets[5]: "Europe moved the other way in the same week."
  Editorial judgement that a WHO roadmap is the opposite of a US deregulatory rule.

- happened[0].bullets[0]: "Two governments entered the record."
  Editorial framing of two documents neither of which, by the same item's account, attributes anything new.

- happened[2].bullets[4]: "The same pattern was measured in biology."
  Editorial equivalence between cyber exploit tests and protein-model reproduction work.

- Quoted string in two wordings: summary[0] "said it had 'not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months'" against happened[0].bullets[7] and unknowns[0] "we have not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months".
  Same ESET sentence quoted two ways in one file.

- Quoted string in two wordings: happened[1].bullets[0] "'impacting at most 5,000 users'" against figures[3] value "at most 5,000 users" and the record's "At most 5,000 users were affected".
  Three renderings of one quotation, attributed to two different speakers across the file.

## 5. OTHER DEFECTS

- happened[0].headline: "Two governments and five vendors place open-source agentic attack frameworks inside live intrusions"
  The second government does not support the claim: by the item's own account Norway's NSM assessment rates national cyber risk and "names no actor", and says nothing about agentic frameworks.

- connects[1].explanation[0]: "The same family of models is named on both sides of the record."
  The stated shared element is not shared — DeepSeek, Kimi and Z.ai's GLM are three different vendors' model families.

- connects[3].explanation[0]: "Anthropic and xAI both switched on invisible text watermarking"
  happened[10].bullets[2] and calendar[2] put xAI's default at 7 November 2026, i.e. after the period and still in the future; happened[10]'s headline makes the same error ("both turn on").

- connects[4].explanation[1]: "Both the Delaware draft and the agent-skills study turn on whether an agent asks before acting"
  The shared element is not shared: per happened[9].bullets[2] the Delaware draft concerns legal personhood, capitalisation and liability shielding, not approval prompts.

- unknowns[7].would_invalidate: "or an independent evaluation showing incident rates falling per unit of deployment."
  Not a concrete observable event — no such denominator or measurement exists in the record.

- unknowns[1].question: "were any of the 5,000 machines actually reached?"
  The record's 5,000 is Cursor's count of affected users, not machines, and the same unknown's evidence_ends concedes no machine count exists.

- figures[3]: value "at most 5,000 users", label "users The Hacker News reports Cursor as saying the tampered Claude Code extension affected on 29 October; Cursor's updated notice carries no count"
  Label misattributes the figure (it is quoted from Cursor's own notice in the record) and asserts an absence the file elsewhere contradicts.

- figures[4]: label "cost Epoch AI reports for building working one-click exploits against each of six Firefox releases with open-weight GLM 5.3"
  Label does not match the value's basis: the item describes a drive-by requiring no user action beyond page load, and the record says every compromise also used an unpublished vulnerability — which already satisfies unknowns[2].would_invalidate ("evidence that the exploits relied on information not available at the Firefox release dates Epoch names"), making that unknown dead on arrival.

- happened[9].editions: ["2026-10-28","2026-10-29","2026-10-31","2026-11-02"] against period {"from":"2026-10-26","to":"2026-11-01"}
  The item cites an edition outside the stated period, and its bullets[3] event (TechCrunch, 1 November) is only in that 2 November edition.

- happened[9].bullets[5] and connects[4].explanation[2]: "TechCrunch does not describe the 'speed limits' as mandatory and gives no detail of what they would cover"
  Presented as the limit of the record, but the 2026-11-02 daily carries Implicator.ai on the same Axios interview stating that "speed limits" means mandatory safeguards for the most powerful AI systems.

input.old_string: Here's the week in three sentences. Two governments put agentic attack frameworks into the official record for the first time, and five security vendors put numbers to them. {"stdout":"AI Edge Briefing - Week in review
The week of 26 October – 1 November 2026

Full week in review: https://aiedgebriefing.com/week/2026-11-02/

Canada's Cyber Centre and six security vendors documented open-source agentic attack frameworks running inside live intrusions. The Cyber Centre said Storm-0940 "used an agentic AI framework known as ARTEX against hundreds of organizations"; CrowdStrike said one ARTEX controller was used against more than 200 distinct organizations in at least 14 countries over 11 days, with a single intrusion's planning agents consuming on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens. ESET, covering April to September 2026, said it had "not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months".
The tools were targets as well. Cursor shut its extension marketplace after two tampered Claude Code builds attempted to plant SSH backdoors, and Wiz counted at least nine AI developer platforms disclosing incidents in October. Anthropic filed to list on Nasdaq as ANT on first-half revenue of $16,286 million, with $131.7 billion of cash and, as CNBC reads the filing, about $417 billion of future compute obligations; on 30 October TechCrunch reported Blackstone telling investors in its $63 billion chip financing to expect a double B range rating. Alphabet reported free cash flow of negative $9,065 million and Amazon an outflow of $42.4 billion, and NBC News reported tech stocks erasing more than $1 trillion in value on Friday.
Epoch AI said the open-weight GLM 5.3 built working Firefox exploits at roughly $1,000 each, and Reuters reported NIST calling it the most capable open-weight model for cybersecurity tasks released to date. HHS finalised the removal of AI model-card requirements from health IT certification against what the rule calls a large majority of commenters; New York's AI companion law for minors became Chapter 368; and the UN First Committee adopted a lethal-autonomous-weapons resolution by 163 to 5 with 9 abstentions. Both OpenAI and Anthropic posted model-generated papers claiming to refute the Exponential Time Hypothesis, hours apart, with the appendix of Anthropic's stating that "at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it".

## 1. What happened
- Canada's Cyber Centre and six vendors place open-source agentic attack frameworks inside live intrusions, one controller used against more than 200 organisations in 11 days
  A government document entered the record for the first time in this story. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's cyber threat bulletin, dated 26 October, says that "Storm-0940 used an agentic AI framework known as ARTEX against hundreds of organizations" and that the actor "moved from selecting a target to gaining privileged access to cloud systems in less than three hours".
